_about: Conformance vectors for external trigger wire parsing and token resolution. The contract: every implementation (JS web player, Kotlin/Android, and any future one) must agree with every vector. If an implementation disagrees, the implementation is wrong. See docs/triggers-design.md.
_why_this_file_exists: The fire path decides whether an unauthenticated packet arriving from a LAN changes what is on a screen. Two implementations of that in two languages will drift, and the drift will be silent and security-relevant — one player accepting a payload another refuses is a hole nobody sees until it is used. Vectors make the contract the artifact and the implementations the thing being checked.

_conventions.wire: ST1 <secret> <token> — exactly three space-separated fields on one line. A trailing \n or \r\n is tolerated because most integrator gear appends one.
_conventions.magic: The literal 'ST1'. Checked before any splitting: on subnet broadcast the socket sees every stray datagram on the LAN, so rejection has to be cheap and bad_magic has to stay meaningful as 'the network is noisy' rather than 'someone is getting it wrong'.
_conventions.token_charset: Printable ASCII 0x21-0x7E, 1-64 chars. No spaces — the payload is space-separated, so a token containing one cannot survive the wire. Refused at save time too, in routes/triggers.js.
_conventions.max_bytes: 512. Bounds the work one datagram can cause.
_conventions.secret: Compared for equality against the per-device shared secret. An absent or empty device secret refuses everything, so an unprovisioned player is inert rather than open.
_conventions.source: 'http' or 'udp'. A trigger that does not accept the arriving transport must not match — enabling only UDP on an alarm says it is fired by the panel wired to it, not by anything that can reach the box over HTTP.
_conventions.scope: The trigger list is already device-scoped by the server at sync time. A token that is real on another screen is simply unknown here.
_conventions.reasons: bad_magic | malformed | too_large | bad_secret | unknown_token. Closed set: these are the counters an installer reads, and 'rejected: 41' without a breakdown answers nothing.
_conventions.precedence: clear_all is checked before per-trigger tokens, so a device-level stop cannot be shadowed by a trigger that happens to use the same token.

vectors.description: a well-formed fire over udp
the same fire over http
a clear token resolves to clear on its own trigger
the device-level clear-all names no trigger
a trailing newline is tolerated — most gear appends one
a trailing CRLF is tolerated too
a UDP-only trigger must NOT fire over http
...and does fire over udp
an HTTP-only trigger must NOT fire over udp
...and does fire over http
the wrong secret is refused
a secret of the right length but wrong content is still refused
a token valid on another screen is simply unknown here
broadcast noise: SSDP
broadcast noise: JSON from something else entirely
an empty datagram
the magic alone, nothing else
a near-miss magic is noise, not malformed
a missing secret field is malformed, not bad_secret — the sender's FORMAT is wrong
a token containing a space cannot be represented on the wire
an empty token
a token with a control character is not printable ASCII
over the 512-byte cap
an unprovisioned device (no secret) refuses everything
with no clear-all configured, that token is just unknown
a device holding no triggers refuses a real token
emergency vs 1000: a head office emergency alert (projected priority 100000 + p, listed FIRST by the server) resolves its own code
emergency vs 1000: listed after an emergency, the store's priority-1000 trigger still resolves its own code — resolution is by token, never by priority
emergency vs 1000: the emergency's clear code resolves to a clear of the emergency
clear_all takes precedence over a trigger using the same token
